The Structured Cabling System: Subsystems, Topology, Distances

Unit 3: Pathways and Spaces. Lesson 10 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

The drawing for a new office floor shows forty outlets, one closet, and a line labeled "to ER." Before you pull anything you need the map of the whole system and the limits it was designed to meet.

The subsystems

Subsystem             What it is
Work area             the outlet, the patch cord, and the equipment on the desk
Horizontal cabling    outlet back to the patch panel in the TR on the same floor
Telecom room (TR)     serves one floor; holds panels, racks, switches, cross-connects
Backbone cabling      links between TRs, equipment rooms, and entrance facilities
Equipment room (ER)   serves the building or campus; large equipment lives here
Entrance facility     where outside cable enters; protectors and the PBB live here

Cabling between two TRs is backbone, even when they are on one floor.

The hierarchical star

Every floor reaches back to a higher level; nothing runs in a ring or a chain. The main cross-connect (MC) is the top, usually in the ER. The intermediate cross-connect (IC) is an optional middle level. The horizontal cross-connect sits in the TR. The horizontal allows one cross-connect level only, with no tandem patch panels between the outlet and the TR. The backbone allows at most two levels. Bridged taps and splices are not allowed in horizontal copper.

Cross-connect or interconnect

A cross-connect joins two cabling runs through patch cords or jumpers. An interconnect connects a run straight to equipment. A consolidation point, at recognition level, is an optional point in the horizontal that serves a cluster of outlets in an open office.

Distances

Horizontal permanent link         90 m (295 ft)
Horizontal channel                100 m (328 ft)
Patch and equipment cords         10 m (33 ft) total

The permanent link is what you build; the channel adds the cords. Never stretch the 90 m to make a run work.

Tip: measure the route, not the straight line. A 70 m wall-to-wall distance can be an 85 m cable route.
Exam tip: 90 + 10 = 100 m. The permanent link is the part you install, and cords add the last 10 m.
Remember
Work area, horizontal, TR, backbone, ER, and entrance facility form a hierarchical star, with 90 m links, 100 m channels, and 10 m of cords.
Deeper explanation

The Structured Cabling System: Subsystems, Topology, Distances, explained slowly

A distance budget for one channel

A channel has a budget, and every meter you spend has to come out of one account or the other. The permanent link has 90 m (295 ft) and the cords have 10 m (33 ft) together. Together that is 100 m (328 ft).

Piece of the channel                   Limit            Example
Horizontal permanent link              90 m  (295 ft)   78 m
Work area cord                         part of 10 m     3 m
Patch cord in the TR                   part of 10 m     2 m
Equipment cord                         part of 10 m     3 m
Cords together                         10 m  (33 ft)    8 m
Channel (link plus cords)              100 m (328 ft)   86 m

Estimating a link before you pull it

Do not scale the straight line on the drawing. A cable runs along a pathway, so add every segment.

Segment                                   Length
TR to the corridor, along the tray        45 m
Corridor to the office, in J-hooks        24 m
Drop down the wall to the outlet           3 m
Service slack at the TR and at the outlet  6 m
Total route                               78 m

Worked example: one passes, one fails

Outlet A has a 78 m route. It is under 90 m, so the permanent link passes. With 8 m of cords the channel is 86 m, under 100 m. Outlet B in the far corner has a route of 92 m. The link is over 90 m, so it fails before any cords are added, and cutting a shorter cord does not save it. You tell the foreman; the designer may add a TR or a TE closer to that corner, or move the outlet.

Never cheat by shortening the cords on paper. The 10 m of cords is a limit on what users may plug in. The application also sets a limit, so the real distance can be shorter than 90 m for a fast service.

Where each distance lives

Subsystem              Where it ends
Work area              the cord ends at the equipment
Horizontal             the outlet to the TR on the same floor
Backbone               TR to TR, TR to ER, and ER to EF

A cross-connect joins two cable runs through patch cords at a panel. An interconnect connects a run straight to the equipment. The horizontal has one cross-connect level and no tandem patch panels, and the backbone allows at most two levels. A bridged tap or a splice in horizontal copper is never allowed.

Remember: 90 + 10 = 100, measure the route, and the permanent link is the part you build.
